title: Degenerative lumbar spondylolisthesis: review of current classifications and proposal of a novel classification system
article_subtype: Review of classification systems, proposal of a new classification, and interobserver and intraobserver reliability assessment
condition_or_topic: Degenerative lumbar spondylolisthesis and its clinical and radiographic classification
clinical_background: Degenerative spondylolisthesis is an acquired spinal condition that can involve instability, spinal stenosis and progressive malalignment. Patients may present with back pain, leg pain, radiculopathy or neurogenic claudication. Although surgery can benefit symptomatic patients, the choice between decompression alone and surgery with stabilization remains uncertain for many patients. Existing classification systems do not fully capture the clinical and radiographic differences that may affect surgical decisions, making it difficult to develop standardized, evidence-based treatment approaches.
objectives: Review established classification systems for degenerative spondylolisthesis.
Propose a classification that incorporates clinically relevant radiographic findings and symptoms to inform surgical decision-making.
Assess interobserver and intraobserver reliability for each component of the proposed classification.
study_design: Review of existing DS classification systems accompanied by a reliability assessment of the proposed UCSF DS classification. After institutional review board approval, 12 observers classified 10 prespecified cases in each of four categories and repeated the assessments 2 weeks later, with the case order randomized in the second round. The observers comprised 4 fellowship-trained spine faculty, 3 fellows, 2 residents, and 3 medical students.

population.description: The reliability assessment used imaging and clinical information from 10 patients who had undergone surgery for L4/5 DS; 6 were male and 4 were female.

primary: Interobserver and intraobserver reliability of the UCSF DS classification categories: segmental dynamic instability, location of spinal stenosis, sagittal alignment, and primary clinical presentation.

statistical_methods: Kappa statistics were calculated separately for each classification category using R, Version 4.2.3. Interobserver reliability was assessed from all observers’ first-round ratings; intraobserver reliability was assessed by calculating a kappa value between rounds for each observer and averaging those values. Agreement was interpreted using the Landis and Koch categories: 0–0.20, slight; 0.21–0.40, fair; 0.41–0.60, moderate; 0.61–0.80, substantial; and 0.81–1.00, near perfect.
interpretation: The authors regard the interobserver and intraobserver agreement across all four UCSF DS categories as nearly perfect. They interpret this agreement as evidence that the classification is straightforward to apply, while its ability to guide treatment remains to be clinically validated.
comparison_with_prior_evidence: Earlier classifications address different subsets of radiographic and clinical features; according to the authors, none incorporates all four UCSF DS categories or formally classifies the location of spinal stenosis. They also note that prior clinical studies and meta-analyses have reported conflicting comparisons of surgical approaches, limiting the development of standardized, evidence-based treatment guidance.
clinical_implications: Separately assessing instability, stenosis location, sagittal alignment and predominant symptoms may distinguish patients whose most suitable surgical approaches differ.

Patients with stable DS, focal neurologic compression and no symptomatic deformity may gain little clinically meaningful benefit from fusion beyond decompression alone, whereas patients with features of instability may benefit from stabilization.
Interbody fusion may be particularly useful when substantial instability, alignment deformity or disc collapse with up/down foraminal stenosis requires correction of structural pathology.
practice_implications: The authors advise against exposing patients with stable DS, focal neurologic compression and no symptomatic deformity to the additional risks of fusion when decompression alone is appropriate.

Fusion may be considered for painful motion segments with mechanical back pain, marked dynamic instability, or a wide decompression likely to destabilize the segment while treating foraminal stenosis.
A more extensive procedure may be needed in the presence of significant dynamic instability, up/down foraminal stenosis and/or regional or global malalignment.
strengths: The proposed system brings together four clinically relevant categories that the authors state had not previously appeared within one classification.
All four categories showed nearly perfect interobserver and intraobserver reliability across case examples representing different DS presentations.
open_questions: Whether the classification can usefully guide treatment choices for patients with DS remains to be established.
The clinical significance of each proposed category and subgroup, including its relative influence on surgical treatment, remains to be determined.
future_directions: Clinically validate the classification and its individual subgroups.
Investigate whether the system can support more standardized, evidence-based treatment approaches and algorithms for selecting surgical strategies.

In the cited Spinal Laminectomy vs. Instrumented Pedicle Screw (SLIP) Trial, revision surgery was more frequent after decompression alone than after posterolateral instrumented fusion among patients with Meyerding Grade 1 DS without overt preoperative instability (34% vs 14%, p = 0.05). The reported revision indications were same-segment instability and junctional complications, respectively.

In the cited study by Inui et al., interbody fusion provided a clinically significant benefit over decompression alone in patients with > 5 mm of preoperative dynamic olisthesis, but not in those with 3-5 mm or < 3 mm.

In the cited Spine Patient Outcomes Research Trial (SPORT), patients whose lower-extremity symptoms predominated had less severe pain at baseline and greater postoperative improvement than those whose low back pain predominated; patients with equally severe symptoms had intermediate outcomes.

main_conclusion: The authors propose UCSF DS as a framework for distinguishing patients with degenerative spondylolisthesis using features relevant to surgical decisions. Its classification domains showed high interobserver and intraobserver agreement, but their clinical relevance and value for guiding treatment still require validation.
narrative_summary:
This article reviews existing classifications of degenerative spondylolisthesis and introduces UCSF DS to account for features that may influence surgical choice: segmental dynamic instability, the location of spinal stenosis, sagittal alignment, and whether leg pain or back pain predominates. Unlike a cumulative score, it considers the domains separately. The authors describe how these features may distinguish patients for whom decompression alone could be appropriate from those who may benefit from fusion or a procedure addressing deformity and up/down foraminal stenosis. These treatment considerations draw on the literature reviewed; the reliability exercise did not test treatment outcomes.

For that exercise, 12 reviewers classified imaging and clinical presentations from 10 surgically treated L4/5 cases, then classified them again 2 weeks later. Interobserver kappa values were 0.94 for dynamic instability, 0.80 for stenosis location, 0.87 for sagittal alignment, and 1.00 for clinical presentation. Corresponding intraobserver values were 0.91, 0.88, 0.87, and 0.97. The authors interpret agreement across the domains as almost perfect. They conclude that the system could support more tailored, standardized surgical decision-making, while emphasizing that its clinical significance and usefulness for directing treatment remain to be validated.

document_sections.heading: Abstract
document_sections.content: The article reviews classifications of degenerative spondylolisthesis (DS), introduces the UCSF DS classification and assesses its interobserver and intraobserver reliability. The proposed system considers segmental dynamic instability, the location of spinal stenosis, sagittal alignment and primary clinical presentation. Its components showed high agreement among and within observers. The authors propose it as a framework for distinguishing patients who may benefit from different surgical strategies; its clinical utility remains to be validated.

document_sections.heading: Purpose
document_sections.content: The objectives were to examine existing DS classification systems, propose one that better represents clinically relevant imaging and clinical characteristics, and measure agreement among and within observers using the new system.

document_sections.heading: Methods
document_sections.content: The proposed classification has four components: 1) segmental dynamic instability, 2) location of spinal stenosis, 3) sagittal alignment, and 4) primary clinical presentation. To assess reliability, 12 observers classified 10 premarked cases twice. Kappa statistics were calculated separately for interobserver and intraobserver agreement on each component.

document_sections.heading: Results
document_sections.content: Interobserver reliability was 0.94 for dynamic instability, 0.80 for stenosis location, 0.87 for sagittal alignment and 1.00 for clinical presentation. Corresponding intraobserver reliability values were 0.91, 0.88, 0.87 and 0.97.

document_sections.heading: Conclusion
document_sections.content: The authors present the UCSF DS classification as a way to assess clinical and radiographic features relevant to surgical treatment. They interpret the nearly perfect interobserver and intraobserver agreement across its components as evidence that it is straightforward to use. It may distinguish otherwise similar patients who could benefit from different treatments and support future surgical decision algorithms. Clinical validation is still needed before it can contribute to more standardized, evidence-based treatment and improved outcomes.

document_sections.heading: Introduction
document_sections.content: DS is an acquired, progressive vertebral subluxation with an intact posterior arch and is a common reason for lumbar surgery in older adults. Unlike dysplastic or isthmic spondylolisthesis, it most characteristically involves anterior displacement of L4 on L5. Disc desiccation alters load distribution and increases facet-joint loading, followed by segmental hypermobility and facet arthropathy. Further degeneration can produce symptomatic lumbar spinal stenosis (LSS), DS and progressive deformity. Structural findings vary and can include central, lateral-recess or foraminal stenosis, instability and malalignment. Patients can present with back pain, leg pain, radiculopathy, sensorimotor deficits or neurogenic claudication, alone or in combination. The authors state that several large randomized trials have established benefits of surgery for symptomatic patients, but the best operation for an individual remains disputed. In particular, when decompression should be combined with stabilization is unclear for many patients and clinicians. The absence of an evidence-based management approach contributes to variation in treatment. Attention to each patient's clinical and radiographic characteristics may help guide care. Because DS encompasses differing structural and symptomatic patterns that may call for different operations, current approaches to diagnosis, treatment and comparison of outcomes may inadequately represent its heterogeneity. The article therefore reviews existing classifications and proposes one intended to capture features important to informed surgical selection.

document_sections.heading: Current systems for classifying DS
document_sections.content: The article examines established ways of classifying DS, including what each describes and which clinically relevant features it leaves out.

document_sections.heading: Overview of current classification methods
document_sections.content: Classification systems can standardize (1) communication between professionals, (2) research and data analysis, (3) treatment selection, and (4) prognosis. Broad adoption also requires ease of use, reliability and clinical relevance. The following systems are considered against those aims.

document_sections.heading: Meyerding classification
document_sections.content: Henry Meyerding introduced this translation-based classification in 1932. Its categories are Grade 1: < 25%; Grade 2: 25–50%; Grade 3: 50–75%; Grade 4: 75–100%; and Grade 5 (spondyloptosis): > 100%. Although simple, reliable and widely recognized, the system has limited ability to distinguish patients with DS: most cases fall into Meyerding grade 1, and displacement rarely exceeds 30%. Slip magnitude and progression correlate poorly with symptoms and treatment response. Translation alone is therefore insufficient to characterize the features needed for clinical decisions.

document_sections.heading: French Society for Spine Surgery (FSSS) classification system
document_sections.content: Proposed in 2014 and adapted from a classification of adult spinal deformity, the FSSS system uses sagittal vertical axis (SVA), L1-S1 lumbar lordosis (LL), segmental lordosis (SL), pelvic incidence (PI) and pelvic tilt (PT). Type 1 denotes normal sagittal alignment, PI-LL < 10°; subtype 1A has preserved SL >5°, whereas 1B has SL <5°. Type 2 denotes compensated malalignment, PI-LL > 10°; subtype 2A has PT < 25° without pelvic compensation, whereas 2B has PT > 25° with pelvic compensation. Type 3 denotes global sagittal malalignment, SVA > 4 cm. Higher FSSS types have been associated with preoperative and postoperative patient-reported health-related quality of life (HRQoL). Although the system provides treatment recommendations, they chiefly concern how worsening malalignment affects procedure choice; other disease-specific structural and clinical influences are not addressed.

document_sections.heading: Clinical and radiographic degenerative spondylolisthesis (CARDS) classification
document_sections.content: Published in 2014, CARDS assigns DS to four types using disc height, vertebral translation and segmental alignment. It also adds a leg-pain modifier outside the principal criteria: 0 for no leg pain, 1 for unilateral pain and 2 for bilateral pain. Type A describes advanced disc collapse without kyphosis; Type B, partially preserved disc height with ≤ 5 mm translation; Type C, partially preserved disc height with > 5 mm translation; and Type D, segmental kyphosis. External validation studies have found CARDS usable and reliable and have highlighted segmental lumbar kyphosis as a predictor of initial symptom severity and potential postoperative improvement. CARDS evaluates the affected segment but not regional or global alignment, despite their possible importance for surgery. Its original description does not give treatment recommendations.

document_sections.heading: Sagittal vertical axis (SVA)
document_sections.content: In a 2019 cross-sectional investigation, Kobayashi et al. grouped patients by SVA using Scoliosis Research Society (SRS)–Schwab Classification thresholds: Type 1, SVA < 40 mm; Type 2, 40 mm ≤ SVA < 95 mm; and Type 3, SVA ≥ 95 mm. They also measured TK, LL, PT, PI and sacral slope (SS), comparing alignment patterns with those of volunteers without lumbar pathology. They found significant spinopelvic differences as global deformity became more severe, informing understanding of malalignment progression in DS. Because clinical disease status and treatment consequences were not examined, the approach offers little direct management guidance.

document_sections.heading: Degenerative spondylolisthesis instability classification (DSIC)
document_sections.content: Proposed in 2015, DSIC is a qualitative aid to selecting an operation according to baseline spinal stability. It arose from a systematic review of biomechanical and clinical stability research and combines back pain, signs of restabilization such as disc-height loss, osteophytes and endplate sclerosis, facet-joint effusion, disc angle and dynamic translation. Its categories link Type I (stable) with decompression alone, Type II (potentially unstable) with decompression and posterior fusion, and Type III (unstable) with decompression, posterior fusion and interbody placement. The underlying review also noted that the relatively low quality of available data restricts evidence-based treatment guidance. DSIC centers the surgical decision on stability without incorporating other structural and clinical determinants.

document_sections.heading: Kulkarni scoring system
document_sections.content: Introduced in 2020 to assess whether patients with DS need fusion, this weighted system recommends fusion when the cumulative score exceeds 5.5. It assigns (+ 2) to mechanical back pain; (+ 1) to age < 70 years; (+ 1) to high-demand activity; (+ 1.5) to segmental kyphosis; (+ 1) to dynamic translation > 2 mm; (+ 1) to disc height > 50% of the adjacent level; (+ 1) to bilateral facet effusion on MRI; (+ 1) to sagittal facet orientation; and (+ 1.5) to the feasibility of decompression without compromising stability. The authors describe the system as reproducible and easy to use but argue that equal total scores can conceal feature combinations that warrant different care. They note that, although its developers give mechanical back pain 2 points and stress its relevance to fusion, many clinicians would regard that pain as an instability indicator warranting fusion regardless of other risk factors.

document_sections.heading: Summary of current classification systems
document_sections.content: Early, widely recognized classifications characterized spondylolisthesis by etiology, as in Wiltse, or by displacement, as in Meyerding. Later DS-specific systems incorporated more features to represent variation in imaging and clinical presentations. Table 1 compares the radiographic and clinical components, advantages and disadvantages of the principal systems. The authors selected four criteria for their proposed system because both clinical and radiographic characteristics affect diagnosis, treatment and prognosis.

document_sections.heading: The UCSF DS classification system
document_sections.content: The proposed system is intended to account for disease-specific features that existing classifications do not consider together when guiding surgical management.

document_sections.heading: Overview of the UCSF DS classification system
document_sections.content: The system is built around four surgical aims: 1. preserving biomechanical stability; 2. relieving neurologic compression; 3. maintaining structural alignment; and 4. alleviating symptoms. It evaluates 1. segmental dynamic instability; 2. location of spinal stenosis; 3. sagittal alignment; and 4. primary clinical presentation. Table 2 shows which of these components occur in earlier classifications, while Table 3 presents the UCSF categories. Each category is considered independently rather than being reduced to a cumulative score. Parameters were selected for their reported relationships with patient-reported HRQoL and their influence on surgical approach. For L4/5 instability, translation is measured between standing radiographs and supine MRI. Lumbar MRI is used to locate central, lateral-recess or foraminal stenosis; foraminal disease is further distinguished by whether up/down narrowing is present, including narrowing from pedicle-on-pedicle contact or osteophytes impinging on the traversing nerve. Segmental alignment, PT and SVA are assessed on 36″ standing radiographs. The VAS scale compares back-pain and leg-pain severity. A symptom with VAS ≥ 4 is designated primary; when both back and leg pain have VAS ≥ 4, the presentation is classified as both leg and back pain.

document_sections.heading: UCSF DS classification system components: rationale
document_sections.content: The authors explain how instability, stenosis location, sagittal alignment and the balance of back and leg symptoms can each affect surgical decisions.

document_sections.heading: Spinal instability
document_sections.content: Maintaining biomechanical stability is a surgical objective in DS. The authors state that concomitant fusion should be performed when disease-related instability or the planned operation creates a high risk of postoperative instability, to prevent recurrent symptoms, progressing deformity and revision surgery. Instrumented fusion is generally preferred because observed fusion-success rates are higher. An interbody device may reinforce the anterior load-bearing column and augment fusion, potentially improving outcomes with excessive segmental mobility. Fusion is nevertheless costlier and more invasive and adds risks of adjacent-segment degeneration and instrumentation complications. Concern about instability has led to fusion in nearly 95% of surgically treated DS cases. Vertebral slip is thought to arise from segmental instability, which can produce symptoms early in the disease; in such cases, adding fusion is suggested to improve symptom relief and prevent related complications. DS can later restabilize, however, and appropriately selected patients can obtain durable relief from decompression alone while avoiding instrumentation risks. Static slip, including its magnitude on the Meyerding classification, does not by itself establish a continuing need for stabilization. Dynamic instability is therefore the usual focus when deciding on fusion. A traditional threshold is > 3 mm of translation on dynamic radiographs; clinical outcome studies also suggest > 5 mm. Inui et al. reported a clinically significant advantage from interbody fusion over decompression alone in patients with preoperative dynamic olisthesis > 5 mm, but not in those with 3-5 mm or < 3 mm. The systematic review underlying DSIC considered both thresholds important in DS.

document_sections.heading: Location of lumbar stenosis
document_sections.content: LSS is pathological narrowing of the central canal, lateral recess or neural foramen and commonly contributes to DS symptoms. Facet arthrosis, reactive ligamentous hypertrophy or disc herniation can cause soft-tissue or bony compression. Direct removal of compressive tissue, traditionally from posteriorly, can often treat uncomplicated central or lateral-recess stenosis through laminectomy, laminotomy or foraminotomy. Foraminal stenosis may instead require wider lateral exposure and partial or complete facet removal. Because facetectomy can destabilize the segment, fusion is often added to prevent iatrogenic instability. In the Spinal Laminectomy vs. Instrumented Pedicle Screw (SLIP) Trial, patients with Meyerding Grade 1 DS without overt preoperative clinical or radiographic instability underwent revision significantly more often after decompression alone involving wide laminectomy and partial facetectomy than after instrumented posterolateral fusion: 34% vs 14%, p = 0.05. Revision indications were same-segment instability in the decompression group and junctional complications in the fusion group, raising concern about surgically induced instability. Foraminal narrowing may be transverse, craniocaudal or circumferential. Hasegawa identified foraminal height less than or equal to 15 mm and posterior disc height less than or equal to 4 mm as significant indicators of lumbar foraminal stenosis. Transverse narrowing can result from dorsal facet disease, ventral foraminal disc protrusion or anterior subluxation of the superior facet; ligamentum flavum hypertrophy and osteophytes can worsen it. Foraminal stenosis without up/down narrowing may be correctable by decompression alone. With more advanced degeneration, disc collapse, olisthesis or malalignment can narrow the foramen vertically. Loss of disc height may bring pedicles into contact, and posterolateral endplate osteophytes may compress the nerve along its foraminal course. Posterior-element resection alone often does not adequately address this up/down stenosis. Distraction with an interbody device can restore disc height, limit ligamentous buckling and indirectly decompress neural structures. Although some foraminal stenosis is amenable to decompression alone, fusion that restores foraminal height can effectively increase foraminal space. Despite its frequency and relevance to symptoms and surgery, stenosis location has not previously been a formal classification component.

document_sections.heading: Sagittal alignment
document_sections.content: The study by Kobayashi et al. describes progressive loss of local, regional and global sagittal balance in DS. Early focal malalignment often appears as altered disc angle at the slipped level. Studies cited by the authors link focal lumbar kyphosis to substantial disability and report a strong response to surgical correction. Untreated focal malalignment can progress to reduced regional lordosis and then greater global deformity. Segmental kyphosis or global malalignment may also reflect posture adopted in response to pain or symptomatic stenosis; treatment decisions therefore require distinguishing structural change from compensation. Because SVA and PT have strong linear correlations with functional outcomes in lumbar pathology, they are commonly used to plan correction and judge its success. In DS, postoperative SVA > 5 cm has been associated with poor outcomes after fusion. High PT has been reported to impair walking function particularly, while inadequate postoperative restoration of balanced pelvic version has been identified as an independent predictor of persistent low back pain. The authors therefore call for assessment of global SVA and PT, regional LL and PI, and focal disc angulation before and after surgery.

document_sections.heading: Clinical presentation
document_sections.content: The relative prominence of low back and leg pain matters for DS treatment and prognosis. The authors describe these symptoms as potentially arising from different processes that require different management. Missing the principal source of pain can lead either to insufficient treatment and relief or to unnecessary treatment and complications. Leg pain and radiculopathy generally indicate focal neural compression and are typically treated most directly by decompressing stenotic sites. Without symptomatic deformity or instability, fusion may offer these patients less additional benefit; decompression alone would be less invasive and more cost-effective. Predominantly mechanical low back pain, by contrast, is often taken as a sign of instability, making stabilization of the painful segment particularly important for relief. Several cited studies reported suboptimal results when patients with low back pain received decompression without fusion. CARDS incorporates leg pain, while DSIC and Kulkarni incorporate back pain, but none assesses their relative severity; that comparison has been shown to predict postoperative functional improvement. In the Spine Patient Outcomes Research Trial (SPORT), predominantly leg-related symptoms were associated with less severe pain at baseline and greater improvement after surgery than predominantly low back pain; patients with equally severe symptoms had intermediate outcomes.

document_sections.heading: Inter/intraobserver reliability
document_sections.content: The article assesses agreement between observers and agreement within the same observer when applying the four UCSF DS components.

document_sections.heading: Methods
document_sections.content: Institutional Investigational Review Board approval preceded the study. Imaging and clinical presentations from 10 surgically treated patients with L4/5 DS were used to test the classification. The 12 evaluators comprised 4 fellowship-trained spine faculty, 3 fellows in training, 2 residents and 3 medical students. The authors found no significant difference in validation accuracy by training level. Reviewers received representative images and relevant measurements and rated each of the four categories 1, 2 or 3. Their example of 4 mm dynamic translation, central but no foraminal stenosis, segmental kyphosis with preserved global alignment, back-pain VAS 6/10 and leg-pain VAS 2/10 receives ratings of 2, 1, 2 and 3, respectively. Each evaluator rated the ten cases again 2 weeks later, with case order randomized in the second round to reduce recall bias. Kappa statistics assessed agreement for each category. Calculations used R, Version 4.2.3 (R Foundation, Vienna, Austria). Interobserver agreement used all first-round ratings to limit familiarity-related bias. For intraobserver agreement, a kappa value was calculated between rounds for each evaluator and the values were averaged. Agreement was interpreted using Landis and Koch: kappa 0–0.20 indicated slight agreement; 0.21–0.40, fair; 0.41–0.60, moderate; 0.61–0.80, substantial; and 0.81–1.00, near perfect.

document_sections.heading: Results
document_sections.content: The 10 cases included 6 males and 4 females; mean age was 64.0 ± 8.5 years. All 12 evaluators rated all 10 cases. Interobserver Fleiss kappa was 0.94 for dynamic instability, 0.80 for stenosis location, 0.87 for sagittal alignment and 1.00 for clinical presentation. Average intraobserver kappa was 0.91, 0.88, 0.87 and 0.97 for those respective categories. Table 4 provides interobserver estimates with 95% CI and average intraobserver estimates with the range across individual evaluators. The authors interpret the results as nearly perfect agreement, although the reported interobserver value for stenosis location is 0.80 and their stated near-perfect Landis and Koch interval begins at 0.81.

document_sections.heading: Discussion
document_sections.content: The UCSF DS categories were designed to reflect fundamental surgical decisions and to separate patients whose best operations may differ. Cited evidence indicates that biomechanically stable patients with focal neural-compression symptoms but no symptomatic deformity have been treated successfully by decompression alone, with low complication and revision rates. The authors consider a clinically meaningful additional benefit from a larger fusion procedure unlikely for this group and advise against exposing them to its added risk. Fusion is considered likely to provide clinically significant benefit in subgroups with instability features. It may stabilize a painful segment in mechanical back pain, prevent progression with pronounced dynamic instability, or protect against instability when adequately treating foraminal stenosis requires wide decompression. Significant dynamic instability, up–down foraminal stenosis or regional or global malalignment may warrant a more extensive operation to correct structural deformity. Interbody fusion can treat discogenic low back pain while increasing stability and fusion rates, adding segmental lordosis and correcting sagittal balance. Its indirect decompressive effect is particularly useful when malalignment or severe disc collapse produces up/down foraminal stenosis. The authors report nearly perfect interobserver and intraobserver reliability across all four categories in varied representative cases. They state that future research must assess the classification's value for guiding treatment and validate the clinical importance of its components and subgroups.

document_sections.heading: Conclusion
document_sections.content: DS is a common contributor to low back pain and disability in older adults. Fusion appears to improve clinical outcomes for some symptomatic patients, whereas others obtain lasting relief with decompression alone. Conflicting comparisons of surgical approaches in clinical studies and meta-analyses have impeded standardized evidence-based guidance. The authors attribute much of that difficulty to heterogeneous clinical and radiographic presentations that existing classifications capture poorly. They propose the UCSF Degenerative Spondylolisthesis Classification System to distinguish patients using a combination of features important to surgical decisions. Further clinical validation is intended to support more standardized, evidence-based treatment and better outcomes.
